name: Ho-Chunk
sweep_summary: the decision rests on the held Helmbrecht 2010 chapter. Seven works with stress in the title, all genuinely about Ho-Chunk word accent: three are duplicate Glottolog records of Hale & White Eagle 1980 (one with wrong pagination 17-34; Crossref: IJAL 46(2):117-132). NEW this search of works with stress in the title: Heiberg 1995 (BLS 21, doi:10.3765/bls.v21i1.1387) was downloaded open from the LSA proceedings site (browser UA required), scanned page by page, and read: it states the placement rule by mora — second mora in bimoraic words, third mora plus alternating secondaries in longer words, Dorsey's Law vowels always high-toned and prominent — which confirms the weight-sensitive exclusion and matches Helmbrecht 2010 rules (1) and (4), re-verified verbatim in the volume PDF we hold (pp.118, 120, 123). Not obtainable openly: Hale & White Eagle 1980, Miner 1979, Miner 1981 (UChicago paywall; OpenAlex's only 'OA' location is the WALS refdb bibliographic record; archive.org holds lending-restricted microfilm scans of the IJAL issues; online with a university library loginper) and Susman 1943 (HathiTrust search-only). Acquisition priority: Hale & White Eagle 1980 high (StressTyp2's own source; the record's 'Stress is final in disyllables' p.118 quote is still second-hand), Miner 1979 medium, Miner 1981 and Susman 1943 low (superseded by Helmbrecht's new data).archive.

new_statements.quote: Hocąk is a mora counting, but syllable accenting language. [...] (1) Primary stress assignment in Hocąk: a. Primary stress falls on the third mora counted from the left boundary of the word. b. If disyllabic words have only two moras (i. e. two syllables with a short vowel as nucleus), primary stress falls on the second mora (i. e. the second syllable). c. Monosyllabic words always have a long vowel, i. e. two moras. Here, stress falls on the first mora.
new_statements.citation: Helmbrecht, Johannes (2010). The accentual system of Hocąk. In Wohlgemuth & Cysouw (eds.), Rara & Rarissima, 117-144. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
new_statements.locator: p. 120, §3.1 'Primary stress', rule (1); heavy-syllable clause p. 118; secondary-stress rule (4) p. 123
new_statements.reading: The most authoritative first-hand statement read this search of works with stress in the title: the language's principal modern documenter, on new project recordings and his own field notes, states primary stress by mora count (third mora from the left; second mora in bimoraic disyllables; first mora in bimoraic monosyllables), with a heavy first/second syllable shifting main stress to the second syllable (p.118) and secondary stress on every even mora after the third (p.123). Placement depends on vowel length / mora structure, so the language cannot be coded as fixed third-syllable stress; the catalog's 'excluded (weight-sensitive)' coding is confirmed. The newly downloaded open source, Heiberg 1995 (BLS 21, pp.152-153), states the same mora-counted rule (second mora in bimoraic words, third mora and alternating secondaries in longer words) on the older published data, so it corroborates rather than rivals this statement. Note the catalog record itself carries empty quote/cite/loc fields: this quote and locator can populate them.

sources.note: Primary description from the Erfurt documentation project's recordings plus fifteen years of the author's own field notes (p.120 preceding text). Third-MORA primary stress; second mora in bimoraic disyllables; first mora in (always bimoraic) monosyllables; p.123 rule (4): words longer than three moras take 'a significant weaker secondary stress on each even numbered mora thereafter'; p.118-119: a heavy first or second syllable puts main stress on the second syllable, yet Hocąk is not weight-sensitive 'per se' since the heavy syllable does not itself attract stress; 'many systematic deviations…

sources.citation: Heiberg, Andrea (1995). A Non-Derivational Approach to Winnebago Stress. Proceedings of the Twenty-First Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 21): 152-161.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: A stressed syllable in Winnebago has higher tone and greater loudness than surrounding syllables (Susman 1943, Miner 1979, White Eagle 1988). There are no monomoraic words (Susman 1943); bimoraic monosyllabic words are realized with a falling tone contour (Susman 1943, Hale and White Eagle 1980 (henceforth HWE)). Stress falls on the second mora of other bimoraic words. [...] In trimoraic and longer words, primary stress falls on the third mora and secondary stresses fall on every other mora thereafter.
sources.locator: §2 'General stress pattern', pp. 152-153 (scanned of PDF pages 2-3)
sources.note: An Optimality-Theory reanalysis built on published data (Susman 1943, HWE 1980, Miner 1979/1990, Lipkind 1945), not new field data. States the placement rule by MORA: second mora in bimoraic words, third mora in longer words, secondary stress on every other mora thereafter; assumes right-headed binary feet built on moras, the leftmost mora unfooted in words of 3+ moras, and feet that may split a long syllable (p.153). Dorsey's Law (epenthetic) vowels are 'always high-toned' and are treated as prominent, shifting footing one mora rightward when they would land in a foot's weak position (pp.155…

sources.quote: 'Ho-Chunk is a mora counting, but syllable accenting language... Two-syllable words have two moras, and primary stress falls on the second mora... In words longer than two syllables, primary stress most often falls on the third syllable, with secondary stress on each even numbered vowel after the point of primary stress... when one of the first two syllables of a multiple-syllable word is a heavy syllable, then the main stress falls on the second syllable.'
